newsitem.title: USA: Mass. county debt not seen hit now by Weld's bill.
newsitem.headline: Mass. county debt not seen hit now by Weld's bill.

text.p: Another move by Massachusetts Gov William Weld to abolish the over 300-year old county system of government was expected to have little impact on $45 million debt issued by them, at least in the near-term.

The governor's decision to send a bill to the legislature that would transfer what he called the essential functions of counties to the state comes on the heels of a default late last year by Middlesex County on about $4.7 million of short-term debt.
Since 1991, more than half the state's 14 counties have received some form of a state bail-out, totaling more than $25 million.

But George Leung, managing director, Moody's Investors Service, noted that whether the legislature will approve the governor's new bill remains unclear, which cushions the effects of any short-term impact. "The mere submission (of the bill) is not going to affect the ratings."

Weld's legislation would end existing county assessments on cities and towns unless they were needed to pay off outstanding county debt. The state would assume all assets and liabilities of the counties.
Leung noted the counties only collect around $27 million in property taxes, a fairly small sum when measured against the state's budget, which runs around $18 billion.
As a result, he predicted Massachusetts was unlikely to suffer any serious financial consequences if the counties were eliminated.

"We are talking about the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, which has substantial resources. I don't mean to downplay the impact...it is an issue for us and we are watching it but the fiscal impacts I think are somewhat limited to the counties," he added.
Neither Standard & Poor's Corp nor Fitch Investors Service rate Massachusetts counties, and thus their analysts declined to comment immediately on the potential impact on Massachusetts.
